concepts.name: SEBI: Statutory Status and Evolution from Non-Statutory Body
key_dimensions: SEBI established as non-statutory body in 1988, given statutory status via SEBI Act 1992 — a common UPSC trap on 'when it became statutory'
Distinction between SEBI as a statutory body vs. a constitutional body — it derives power from an Act of Parliament, NOT the Constitution
Comparison with RBI (also statutory but under RBI Act 1934) to avoid confusion in MCQs
SEBI's headquarters in Mumbai and its quasi-legislative, quasi-executive, and quasi-judicial character simultaneously

concepts.name: SEBI's Triple Role: Legislative, Executive, and Judicial Functions
key_dimensions: Quasi-legislative: Power to frame regulations (e.g., SEBI (LODR) Regulations, insider trading norms)
Quasi-executive: Power to investigate, inspect books of accounts, conduct searches — acts like an enforcement arm
Quasi-judicial: Power to pass orders, impose penalties, issue cease-and-desist orders — SAT (Securities Appellate Tribunal) provides the appellate check
UPSC trap: SAT appeal lies to Supreme Court directly (not High Court) — critical exception to normal appellate hierarchy

concepts.name: SEBI's Powers of Adjudication and Penalties
key_dimensions: Adjudicating Officer appointed by SEBI to hold inquiry and impose monetary penalties
Types of violations: insider trading, fraudulent trade practices, failure to furnish information — each has specific penalty ceilings
Recovery of penalties as 'arrears of land revenue' — an important procedural angle
Appeal chain: Adjudicating Officer → SAT → Supreme Court (bypassing High Courts — a frequent MCQ trap)

concepts.name: Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT): Composition and Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: SAT is a statutory tribunal under SEBI Act — not a constitutional tribunal; presided by a Presiding Officer with judicial background
Jurisdiction: Appeals against SEBI orders AND Insurance Regulatory orders (IRDAI) — a critical overlap that UPSC exploits
SAT does NOT hear appeals against RBI orders — a common distractor in MCQs
Presiding Officer qualifications: Must be a sitting or retired Judge of a High Court — not Supreme Court

concepts.name: TRAI: Establishment, Composition, and the TRAI-DOT Conflict
key_dimensions: TRAI established under TRAI Act 1997; reconstituted in 2000 after Supreme Court ruling striking down original TRAI's judicial powers
Separation of regulatory and disputes-settlement functions: TRAI for regulation; TDSAT (Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal) for disputes — a key structural distinction
TRAI's advisory role to the Central Government on telecom matters is recommendatory, NOT binding — a UPSC trap
Historical DOT-TRAI conflict: Department of Telecom was both a service provider and regulator before TRAI — restructuring led to creation of BSNL

concepts.name: TDSAT: Jurisdiction, Composition, and Overlap with TRAI
key_dimensions: TDSAT adjudicates disputes between licensor (government) and licensees, between service providers, and between service providers and consumers (groups, not individuals)
Individual consumer complaints do NOT go to TDSAT — they go to consumer forums under Consumer Protection Act — a high-yield trap
TDSAT also hears appeals against TRAI orders — dual role of dispute settlement AND appellate body
Appeal from TDSAT lies to Supreme Court (not High Court) — mirrors SAT's appellate route, both bypass High Courts

concepts.name: TRAI's Recommendatory and Regulatory Powers: Binding vs. Advisory
key_dimensions: TRAI can make recommendations on its own OR when referred by the Central Government on: need for new service providers, terms of licenses, measures for technological improvement
Government can reject recommendations but MUST give reasons in writing — a procedural safeguard often tested
TRAI cannot impose penalties directly — it regulates tariffs, quality of service, and issues directions; punitive action is limited
TRAI's power to call for information from service providers is quasi-executive, but it lacks independent prosecution powers unlike SEBI

concepts.name: IRDAI: Statutory Basis, Composition, and Dual Mandate
key_dimensions: IRDAI established under IRDA Act 1999, based on Malhotra Committee recommendations (1994) — origin and rationale are frequently tested
Regulates both Life Insurance and General Insurance — including health insurance (a common misconception that health insurance falls under a separate body)
Composition: Chairperson + not more than 5 whole-time members + not more than 4 part-time members — specific numbers are MCQ-ready
IRDAI's headquarters: Hyderabad (shifted from Delhi in 2001) — geography of regulatory bodies is a recurring MCQ theme

concepts.name: IRDAI's Powers: Licensing, Investment Regulation, and Consumer Protection
key_dimensions: IRDAI grants Certificate of Registration to insurance companies — without it, no insurer can operate; renewal, modification, suspension, and cancellation powers
Investment regulations: IRDAI mandates insurers to invest specified proportions in government securities and social sector — links to financial inclusion mandate
Grievance redressal: Insurance Ombudsman system works parallel to IRDAI — IRDAI sets the framework but Ombudsman is independent
IRDAI regulates Insurance Repositories and Insurance Brokers — intermediary regulation is a less-tested but high-yield dimension

concepts.name: Overlapping Jurisdiction: SEBI vs. IRDAI on ULIPs
key_dimensions: 2010 ULIP controversy: Both SEBI and IRDAI claimed jurisdiction over Unit Linked Insurance Plans — a landmark regulatory conflict
Resolution: Finance Minister invoked Section 16 of SEBI Act allowing government to resolve jurisdiction disputes; ultimately ULIPs kept under IRDAI
Legislative fix: Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act 2015 clarified IRDAI's exclusive jurisdiction over insurance products
Lesson for UPSC: When two regulators overlap, the government (Finance Ministry) acts as the arbitrator — not courts in the first instance

concepts.name: Financial Sector Regulatory Coordination: FSDC and Inter-Regulatory Overlaps
key_dimensions: Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) established in 2010 to coordinate among SEBI, IRDAI, RBI, PFRDA — chaired by Finance Minister (not RBI Governor, a common trap)
FSDC is NOT a statutory body — it has no legislative backing, making it weaker than individual regulators
PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority) under PFRDA Act 2013 — sometimes confused with IRDAI for pension-cum-insurance products
Jurisdictional clarity: Banking (RBI), Securities (SEBI), Insurance (IRDAI), Pension (PFRDA) — UPSC tests inter-body boundary cases

concepts.name: Appointment, Tenure, and Removal of Heads of Regulatory Bodies
key_dimensions: SEBI Chairperson: Appointed by Union Government; tenure 5 years or until age 65, whichever is earlier — reappointment NOT allowed (ensures independence)
TRAI Chairperson: Appointed by Union Government; tenure 3 years or until age 65; eligible for reappointment — contrast with SEBI
IRDAI Chairperson: Appointed by Union Government; tenure 5 years or until age 65; NOT eligible for reappointment

Removal: All three can be removed by the Central Government on grounds of insolvency, conviction, unsound mind, or if 'public interest' requires — the 'public interest' ground is vague and controversial from independence standpoint

concepts.name: Statutory Bodies vs. Constitutional Bodies vs. Executive Bodies: Classification Traps
key_dimensions: SEBI, TRAI, IRDAI are ALL statutory bodies (created by Acts of Parliament) — NOT constitutional bodies like CAG, UPSC, Election Commission
Executive bodies created by Cabinet Resolution (e.g., old SEBI in 1988, Planning Commission, NITI Aayog) have no statutory backing — can be dissolved by executive order alone
Quasi-judicial character: All three exercise judicial-like functions but are NOT courts; their orders are subject to appeal to statutory tribunals (SAT, TDSAT) and then Supreme Court
UPSC trap: 'Which of the following is a constitutional body?' — inserting SEBI or TRAI as distractors alongside CBI (also NOT constitutional) or CVC (statutory)

concepts.name: SEBI and Insider Trading Regulations: Scope and Recent Amendments
key_dimensions: SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations 2015 replaced 1992 regulations — definition of 'insider' and 'Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)' broadened
Connected persons and deemed connected persons — vicarious liability concept imported into securities regulation
SEBI's 2018 amendment introduced informant mechanism (whistleblower rewards) — links to anti-corruption governance questions
SEBI vs. CBI jurisdiction on insider trading: SEBI handles civil/regulatory penalties; CBI can handle criminal prosecution under SCAM — dual-track enforcement

concepts.name: TRAI and Net Neutrality: Regulatory Philosophy and Global Comparison
key_dimensions: TRAI's 2016 order prohibiting differential pricing for data services — landmark net neutrality ruling, struck down Facebook's Free Basics in India
2018: Government formally incorporated net neutrality principles into telecom licenses following TRAI recommendations — regulatory recommendation becoming licensing condition
India's net neutrality framework: Prohibits blocking, throttling, paid prioritization — aligns with EU model rather than US (where FCC repealed net neutrality in 2017)
TRAI's role is recommendatory on licensing — actual license conditions set by DOT; demonstrates the regulator-government relationship tension

concepts.name: Regulatory Independence vs. Government Control: Structural Safeguards and Criticisms
key_dimensions: Financial autonomy: SEBI's income from fees (not government grants) — greater financial independence than TRAI which depends partly on government funding
Revolving door problem: Former government officials appointed to head regulators, and vice versa — compromises arm's-length relationship
Fali Nariman Committee and FSLRC (Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission 2013) recommendations: Unified Financial Code, independent regulators with fixed non-renewable terms
Parliamentary oversight: Annual reports tabled in Parliament; PAC can examine — but no dedicated parliamentary committee exclusively for financial regulators

concepts.name: SEBI's Role in Primary and Secondary Markets: Distinct Regulatory Instruments
key_dimensions: Primary market regulation: SEBI mandates prospectus disclosures, DRHP filing, IPO pricing norms — SEBI Act + Companies Act 2013 overlap here
Secondary market: Regulation of stock exchanges (NSE, BSE) as 'recognized stock exchanges' under SEBI oversight — exchanges themselves are self-regulatory organizations (SROs)
SEBI's oversight of credit rating agencies, depositories (NSDL, CDSL), and portfolio managers — breadth of SEBI's regulated entities is a frequent MCQ dimension
Market surveillance: Algorithmic trading regulations, circuit breakers — SEBI's powers extend to trading technology governance

concepts.name: Insurance Regulatory Architecture: Ombudsman, Surveyors, and IRDAI's Indirect Regulation
key_dimensions: Insurance Ombudsman: Appointed under Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017; handles individual grievances up to ₹30 lakh — NOT appointed by IRDAI but by Executive Council of Insurers (Governing Body of Insurance Council)
IRDAI does NOT directly adjudicate individual consumer complaints — a critical trap distinguishing IRDAI's macro-regulatory role from consumer redressal
Licensed surveyors and loss assessors: IRDAI licenses them — intermediary regulation dimension
Reinsurance regulation: General Insurance Corporation (GIC Re) is India's national reinsurer; IRDAI regulates foreign reinsurance branches operating in India

concepts.name: Spectrum Allocation and TRAI's Advisory Role vs. DOT's Executive Role
key_dimensions: Supreme Court's 2012 2G Spectrum Judgment: Quashed 122 telecom licenses; held that spectrum is a public resource and allocation must follow transparent process — TRAI's recommendations had been bypassed
National Frequency Allocation Plan (NFAP) made by DOT; TRAI recommends spectrum pricing and auction methodology — allocation power stays with government, not TRAI
TRAI's recommendations on spectrum are binding in the sense that government must respond, but not binding in the sense that government must comply
Intersection with competition law: CCI (Competition Commission of India) can investigate telecom mergers independently of TRAI — dual regulatory oversight

concepts.name: Comparison Matrix: SEBI vs. TRAI vs. IRDAI — Key Structural Differences
key_dimensions: Appellate body: SEBI → SAT; TRAI → TDSAT; IRDAI → SAT (IRDAI shares SAT with SEBI — a high-yield trap, no separate appellate tribunal for insurance)
Penalty powers: SEBI has strong direct penalty powers; TRAI's penalty powers are limited and channeled through TDSAT; IRDAI can impose penalties on insurers directly
Sector coverage: SEBI = capital markets only; TRAI = telecom + broadcasting; IRDAI = life + non-life + health + reinsurance insurance

Self-regulatory organizations (SROs) under each: SEBI → Stock Exchanges, AMFI; TRAI → none (DOT retains more direct control); IRDAI → Insurance Council (Life and General) — SRO landscape differs significantly
